can.cut: Ich kann mit der Schere schneiden

englishSourceNotes: 'I can catch a fish' states an outcome, not a skill a child reliably has; 'I can go fishing' is more honest. German uses 'einen Fisch angeln' (the act of fishing).

'My favorite clothes' (plural) heads a row where the child circles ONE garment; 'My favorite piece of clothing' is more accurate. German uses the mass noun 'Kleidung', which reads naturally either way.

'My favorite bug' covers a snail, a worm and a spider, none of which are insects; acceptable colloquial English, but German deliberately uses 'Krabbeltier' (the Kita word for all small crawling creatures) rather than 'Insekt'.
'My favorite treat' mixes sweets with cake, pancake and waffle; fine in English. German 'Süßigkeit' would exclude cake/pancake, so 'Leckerei' is used.
'I can play a board game' is cued by a single die; acceptable, but a board picture would match better.

'I can draw a picture' collides in German with the shipped paint sentence 'Ich kann ein Bild malen' (malen = both paint and draw for children); German draw is therefore 'mit Stiften zeichnen', matching the crayon cue.
'My favorite shape' offers moon and heart, which are not geometric shapes; fine for 5-year-olds — German uses 'Form', not 'geometrische Figur'.

optionWordFlags.problem: 'Brei' alone suggests baby food/mush; the German breakfast word is 'Haferbrei' (or 'Porridge').
Picture is a single small sausage; 'Würstchen' is the natural breakfast word. 'Wurst' reads as cold cuts.
Picture shows cereal rings in a bowl, not Müsli (oats, nuts, raisins); 'Cornflakes'/'Frühstücksflocken' would match. Acceptable but imprecise.

In Berlin and much of eastern Germany 'Pfannkuchen' means a jam doughnut (Berliner). The picture is a stack of American pancakes; still the best nationwide word, but regionally ambiguous. Same for breakfast/pancake.
Correct but adult register; a 5-year-old says 'Zelten' (and the picture is a tent).
Correct; children more often say 'Krake'. Minor.
Missing German word; should be 'Meerschweinchen' (a very popular child's pet in Germany — worth keeping).
Missing German word; 'Zuckerstange'. Culturally marginal in Germany — fine to drop.
Missing German word; should be 'Ei' (the classic Frühstücksei).

otherNotes: Heading pattern follows shipped 'Mein Lieblingstier' / 'Meine Lieblingsfarbe' (Lieblings- compound, article by gender). Two headings use 'liebste(s)' + noun instead: 'Meine liebste Leckerei' and 'Mein liebstes Bauernhoftier' (the compound 'Lieblingsbauernhoftier' is unreadable for a 5-year-old and cannot wrap).

Length: 'Mein Lieblingsinstrument' (24), 'Mein Lieblingsmeerestier' (24), 'Mein Lieblingskrabbeltier' (25), 'Meine Lieblingskleidung' (23), 'Mein Lieblingsfrühstück' (23), 'Mein liebstes Bauernhoftier' (27) exceed 22 chars but break into two lines at the space; the longest unbreakable word is 'Lieblingskrabbeltier' (20). German compounds cannot be shortened without losing meaning — please confirm the box fits a 20-char word on one line.

'Ich kann mit der Schere schneiden' is 33 chars (under hard max 34); shorter forms drop the scissors the cue shows. 'Ich kann meinen Rucksack packen', 'Ich kann meine Stiefel anziehen' and 'Ich kann Drachen steigen lassen' are 31 chars; no natural shorter form exists.
coat: the picture is a buttoned coat (Mantel), but German children say 'Jacke'; 'Ich kann meine Jacke zuknöpfen' is used deliberately for everyday child speech (30 chars).
bounce: 'dribbeln' is the word children know from ball games; 'prellen' is regional/school-sport jargon.
slide: 'Ich kann rutschen' — with the slide picture the meaning is unambiguous; 'auf der Rutsche rutschen' is repetitive.
All sentences keep the shipped 'Ich kann …' first-person pattern with no final period, as in the shipped can entries.

Follow-up revisions (US panel audit): tidy → 'Ich kann den Boden fegen' (broom cue); coat → 'zuknöpfen'; swing → 'allein schaukeln'; draw → 'Ich kann sauber ausmalen' ('sauber ausmalen' is the Kita/Grundschule phrase for colouring inside the lines). bake kept: 'Ich kann beim Backen helfen' fits a whisk (stirring the dough).
